title: Will there ever be a new programming language?
summaryRaw:
For as long as I can remember, about once a week or so someone on Hacker News introduced their pet project, a new programming language. It almost seems like a rite of passage to, for some period at least, believe that you can beat the odds and come up with a way of presenting information that improves upon present methods and, just perhaps, goes viral and changes the world of software by some measurable increment.
Will this tendency to reinvent the wheel survive the transition to AI-driven software development? What would be the impetus, when everyone is programming in English (or some other human language), and the 'compiler' has a higher IQ than the 'programmer'? Note that any new language will by definition not be in the corpus of information any frontier model was trained on.
I feel (fear?) we are basically locked in to a world where C, C++, Rust, Go, Python and Javascript will be the assembly code we compile to, and there will be no path or even raison dêtre to improve or innovate

Encode credentials or pass a token. A raw / or # in the password makes the ProxyAgent constructor throw invalid url; encodeURIComponent each part or use the token option.
Use undici 7.28.0 or 8.

summaryRaw:

It is the textbook NP-complete problem, which is usually where the lesson stops. In theory it is hard. title: Show HN: DragDropMath – Learn math by feel
summaryRaw:
Hi HN!
I am a professional physicist and I shuffle symbols in equations and mathematical expressions all day long. During my PhD (almost 20 years ago) I noticed that it is as if the symbols have their own 'physics', which makes the wrong moves impossible and the right ones obvious.
So I created DragDropMath, where you can learn how to simplify mathematical expressions and how to solve equations by dragging symbols around, and only correct moves are allowed, so you get to feel what's right without experiencing (and so learning) wrong moves.
I always wanted to make this, but life got in the way. Then a few weeks ago I saw declarative dragging (https://declarative-dragging.github.io/) on the front page of HN and the spark came back!
It took quite a few rounds to get the feel right, but I think it's close to what happens in my mind when I mentally manipulate these expressions.

title: Show HN: bouncemarket – a live prediction market game for a bouncing ball
summaryRaw:
a ball will fall. trade on where it lands.
I made this game! Some technical details:
The entire drop of the ball is simulated server-side, then streamed to each client as server-sent events with a small buffer. Every drop is deterministic from its starting position, so rounds can be replayed exactly for later analysis, but tiny variations in starting position can change the ultimate outcome.
There's some AI traders to keep the market moving, but they drop out in any round that has more than five people. They operate using a naive set of rules that I wrote for them, so they're not too hard to beat -- it's when the market is full of real people that it gets tricky.
Curious to get feedback on anything you would change, and especially whether the mechanics were clear right away or not.

title: Sheetlytic – Take a photo of sheet music and hear it play
summaryRaw:
My wife is a piano teacher, and she often encounters a simple problem: students return home after their lessons and forget how a piece is supposed to sound or how a particular passage should be played.
I built Sheetlytic, an app that turns a photo of sheet music into playable music.
The idea is to bridge the gap between reading sheet music and hearing it, without having to search for an existing recording or manually enter notes into notation software.
While the original motivation came from piano teaching, I think it could also be useful for musicians learning unfamiliar pieces on their own.
Sheetlytic is available on:
Android: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=verbosus.sheetlytic
iOS: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/sheet-music-scanner-player/id6830832313
Windows: https://apps.microsoft.com/detail/9p2pm166vc69
I'm the developer and would love to hear your feedback, particularly on usability, recognition accuracy, and potential use cases.
Happy to answer any questions!

title: Tiny Hat: a new Linux distro dedicated to retro gamedev
summaryRaw:
Tiny Hat uses only around 100MB of RAM after booting, and can be booted from a >= 1GB memory stick. It comes with a few small games, an easy way to install and run more games and several example programs for getting into retro game development. It also uses a modern stack of libraries, with dwl / Wayland, SDL3 and GTK4.
One possible use is to buy a cheap x86 machine for younger members of a family, to completely brain wash inspire them into getting into graphics programming and appreciating retro games, perhaps as a Christmas present.
At least a few people have found it fun so far, so I wanted to share it.
